meta.description: Audrey Hepburn is universally credited, but this pun appears in nothing she said or wrote. It's an unsourced, anonymous aphorism — Wikiquote and Goodreads flag it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing is impossible, the word itself says I'm possible'?
meta.ogDescription: Audrey Hepburn gets the credit, but the line is in no documented speech, interview, book or letter. An unsourced modern aphorism — the evidence.

answer.label: Not Audrey Hepburn — an unsourced modern aphorism
answer.authorName: Unknown — an anonymous piece of wordplay
answer.authorDates: Popularly pinned to Audrey Hepburn (1929–1993), who left no record of saying it
answer.sourceLine: This “impossible / I’m possible” pun is universally credited to Audrey Hepburn, but it is documented in none of her interviews, speeches, books, or letters. Wikiquote carries it only as an unsourced attribution, and Goodreads tags it “attributed-no-source.” No verified originator is known — it reads as anonymous motivational wordplay later attached to her name.

source.excerpt: Nothing is impossible, the word itself says ‘I’m possible’!
trail: Wikiquote’s talk page logs this line among unsourced attributions to Hepburn; it is absent from every sourced section of her main Wikiquote entry.
Goodreads hosts it with tens of thousands of likes but tags it “attributed-no-source.”
Hepburn is a documented magnet for false quotes: Wikiquote’s talk page documents that the famous “beauty tips” verse was Sam Levenson’s, not hers.
Quote Investigator has traced other “nothing is impossible” quips but not this Hepburn line — no researcher has found a primary source for it.
source.excerptNote: The line trades entirely on splitting the written word impossible into I’m possible — a play that only works in English and has circulated anonymously on posters, cards, and social media, most often under Hepburn’s name.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identifiable first publication or author — it is an anonymous motivational aphorism of uncertain date circulated on posters, cards, and the web. With no sourced work to date, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted; it is neither demonstrably public-domain nor tied to a known rights holder.

author.name: Audrey Hepburn
author.heading: Audrey Hepburn — the credited, not the author
author.bio: Audrey Hepburn was the Belgian-born British actress of Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany’s, and My Fair Lady, and in her later years a devoted UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. Her luminous public image made her a magnet for feel-good quotations she never actually said — from the “beauty tips” that were really Sam Levenson’s to this “I’m possible” pun. The optimism fits her legend, which is precisely why the misattribution sticks.

misattribution.heading: Why Hepburn gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most-shared “Audrey Hepburn” quotes, yet the attribution rests on nothing but repetition. It follows the same pattern as her other famous fake quotes.

items.why: Credited to her across BrainyQuote, Goodreads, and countless posters, but with no interview, speech, book, or letter behind it. Goodreads itself tags it “attributed-no-source.”

The “impossible / I’m possible” split is a stock English pun that circulated anonymously before being attached to Hepburn’s name; no documented originator has been identified by Quote Investigator or Wikiquote.

The “For beautiful eyes, look for the good in others” verse endlessly credited to Hepburn was actually Sam Levenson’s; Wikiquote’s talk page documents that she recited it but did not write it — the same dynamic that produced this fake.

misattribution.truthLine: No primary source connects this pun to Audrey Hepburn; it survives only through repetition, and Wikiquote lists it as unsourced.

context.heading: A pun that outran its author
lead: The appeal is mechanical: the word impossible literally contains the letters of I’m possible, so the aphorism feels like it reveals a hidden truth. That tidy, screenshot-ready cleverness is exactly what powers a modern viral quote — and exactly why it needed a glamorous, optimistic face to travel under.

Audrey Hepburn, beloved and safely beyond correction, became the default attribution the same way she did for Sam Levenson’s beauty verse. The line likely predates its Hepburn branding as anonymous poster-and-greeting-card wisdom, but without a datable first appearance, honesty requires calling it what it is: unsourced.
context.pull: “Impossible” really does spell “I’m possible” — but Audrey Hepburn is not on record saying so.
